# **Molecular Structure of Biological Molecules**

**Carbohydrates, Lipids, Proteins, Nucleic Acids, and Functional Groups**

Estimated Time: 2.5--3 hours

## **Introduction: Molecular Structure of Biological Molecules**

Living organisms are composed of many organic molecules, most of which can be grouped into four major biological classes: **carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids**. These molecules are central to life because they store energy, provide structural support, regulate cellular processes, form membranes, catalyze reactions, and carry genetic information.

Many biological molecules are built from smaller units. For example, simple sugars called **monosaccharides** may exist as individual molecules or join to form disaccharides and polysaccharides. **Amino acids** link together to form polypeptides and proteins. **Nucleotides** form nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA. Lipids are more chemically diverse; some contain fatty acids and glycerol, while others, such as sterols, contain fused carbon rings.

In this laboratory, you will examine molecular models and structural formulas representing the four major classes of biological molecules. You will identify functional groups, compare molecular structures, and relate structure to biological functions. As you work, focus on how atoms, bonds, polarity, molecular shape, and subunit arrangement influence what each molecule does in living systems.

For a direct and concise review of this topic you con review the following review on the macromolecules: [Macromolecules - Classes and Functions](https://youtu.be/V5hhrDFo8Vk?si=FMZE6Rc60Z9bBpFD) from the 2-Minute Classroom

**Learning Objectives**

By the end of this laboratory, students should be able to:

1.  Identify the four major classes of biological molecules.

2.  Recognize common subunits of carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids.

3.  Compare monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides.

4.  Distinguish among major lipid types, including fatty acids, triglycerides, phospholipids, and sterols.

5.  Identify the general structure of an amino acid and explain the importance of the R group.

6.  Describe the basic structure of nucleotides, DNA, and RNA.

7.  Identify common functional groups in biological molecules.

8.  Explain how molecular structure relates to biological functions.

## **Part I. Carbohydrates: Sugars and Polysaccharides**

**Suggested Time: 35--40 minutes**

Carbohydrates are composed primarily of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Many carbohydrates contain multiple hydroxyl groups, making them polar and often water-soluble. Carbohydrates may function as immediate energy sources, energy-storage molecules, or structural materials. This topic may be reviewed in "[Carbohydrates,; biological molecules simplified #1](https://youtu.be/PADu-fA7vfA?si=LgidDHhfx-r2JEPQ)"

**A. Monosaccharides: Glucose**

Glucose is a six-carbon monosaccharide with the molecular formula: C~6~H~12~O~6~

Glucose may be represented in a linear or ring form. Ring forms are common in aqueous environments. Different ring arrangements of glucose can produce structural isomers, such as alpha-glucose and beta-glucose.

![What is Carbohydrates? - Foods, Healthy Carbs for Weight Loss](data:image/jpeg;base64,){width="2.612346894138233in" height="1.7833639545056867in"} ![http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/27/D-glucose-chain-2D-Fischer.png](data:image/png;base64,){width="0.978338801399825in" height="1.6794477252843394in"}

> Figure 4.1a: a glucose molecule Figure 4.11b: a linear glucose molecule

Two diagrams of glucose are shown: Figure 4.1a presents glucose as a ring-shaped molecule, while Figure 4.1b shows it as a straight-chain molecule, illustrating its two common forms.

**Figure 4.1a: Ring (cyclic) glucose molecule**\
A ring-shaped glucose molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆) is shown in its cyclic form, where the carbon chain has folded to form a six-membered ring. This occurs when the aldehyde group at carbon 1 reacts with the hydroxyl group on carbon 5. The ring consists of five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, with hydroxyl (--OH) groups attached to the carbons. The position of the --OH group on carbon 1 distinguishes α- and β-glucose forms.

**Figure 4.1b: Linear glucose molecule**\
A linear glucose molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆) is shown in its open-chain form, consisting of a six-carbon backbone with an aldehyde group (--CHO) at carbon 1 and hydroxyl (--OH) groups attached to the remaining carbons. This structure can cyclize in solution to form the ring structure shown in Figure 4.1a.

Credits: Figure 4.1a & 4.1b: From <https://www.nutrientsreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/09/Glucose-formula.jpg>

**Figure 4.2** (Glucose Isomers: α-glucose and β-glucose):\
A diagram showing two ring-shaped glucose molecules labeled α-glucose and β-glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆). Both structures consist of six-membered rings made of carbon and oxygen atoms with attached hydroxyl (--OH) groups. The key difference is the orientation of the --OH group on carbon 1: in α-glucose it points downward, while in β-glucose it points upward. .

**B. Disaccharides: Sucrose**

Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides are joined by a **glycosidic linkage**. Sucrose is a common disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose.

During the formation of a disaccharide, water is removed. During breakdown of a disaccharide, water is added in a process called **hydrolysis**.

![https://www.chem.purdue.edu/jmol/molecules/sucrose.gif](data:image/png;base64,){width="2.7650393700787403in" height="1.4106867891513561in"} ![Skeletal formula of sucrose](data:image/png;base64,){width="2.623137576552931in" height="1.3588790463692038in"}

(4.3a) (4.3b)

**Figure 4.3a & 4.3b (Sucrose molecule representations):**\
Two diagrams of a sucrose molecule are shown. The first (2a) is a detailed structural model displaying all atoms, including carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen, clearly illustrating the glucose and fructose units joined by a glycosidic bond. The second (2b) is a simplified skeletal diagram where carbon atoms and attached hydrogens are not shown; instead, lines are bonds and the overall structure, making the arrangement of the two sugar rings easier to see.

**Figure 4.3 a & b:** Sucrose molecules. Figure 2a contains all the hydrogens in the molecule. From <https://www.chem.purdue.edu/jmol/molecules/sucrose.gif> Figure 2b is the chemist's shorthand version. From <https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Saccharose2.svg/440px-Saccharose2.svg.png>

## **Part II. Lipids: Fatty Acids, Triglycerides, Phospholipids, and Sterols**

**Suggested Time: 40--45 minutes**

Lipids are a diverse group of mostly hydrophobic molecules. Many contain long hydrocarbon regions, which make them poorly soluble in water. Lipids function in long-term energy storage, insulation, membrane structure, waterproofing, and chemical signaling. A brief introduction may be seen in the following video: "[Lipids \| Fats, Steroids, and Phospholipids \| Biological Molecules Simplified #4"](https://youtu.be/69-eGO7XDfU?si=6dSIsmtbzVqlXgYo)

**A. Fatty Acids**

Fatty acids contain a carboxyl group at one end and a hydrocarbon chain. A **saturated fatty acid** contains no carbon-carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain. An **unsaturated fatty acid** contains one or more carbon-carbon double bonds, often producing bends in the chain.

**C. Phospholipids**

![molecular structure of phospholipid Figure 2.  ](data:image/png;base64,){width="3.676654636920385in" height="3.287777777777778in"}

A diagram of a phospholipid molecule showing a polar head group and two nonpolar fatty acid tails. The head has a phosphate group, while the tails extend as long hydrocarbon chains, illustrating the molecule's structure with a water-attracting (hydrophilic) head and water-repelling (hydrophobic) tails.

**Figure 4.7;** a phospholipid. From <https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Ebrahim-Zahrabi/publication/297161568/figure/fig1/AS:336950331494401@1457346627123/molecular-structure-of-phospholipid-Figure-2.png>

Phospholipids are major components of cell membranes. A phospholipid has a hydrophilic head region and hydrophobic fatty acid tails. Because it has both water-attracting and water-repelling regions, it is described as **amphipathic**.

4.  Predict how phospholipids arrange themselves in water.

5.  Explain why phospholipids are well suited for membrane formation.

**D. Sterols**

Sterols are lipids with a characteristic four-ring carbon framework. Cholesterol is the major sterol in animal cells. It contributes to membrane structure and serves as a precursor for several important molecules, including steroid hormones and vitamin D.

## **Part III. Proteins: Amino Acids and Polypeptides**

**Suggested Time: 35--40 minutes** **PROTEINS: Pages 75-83**

Proteins are polymers made of amino acid monomers. Each amino acid contains a central carbon attached to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom, and an R group. The R group differs among amino acids and determines many of their chemical properties.

Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds to form polypeptides. The amino acid sequence influences how the protein folds, and the folded shape determines protein function. For a quick review please visit the following video: "[Proteins, Biological Molecules simplified #2"](https://youtu.be/mEROyfRxbFM?si=Py4gt7dfXwW6B3IZ)

## **Part IV. Nucleic Acids: Nucleotides, DNA, and RNA**

**Suggested Time: 35--40 minutes** **NUCLEIC ACIDS** **Pages 84-87, 260**

Nucleic acids store and transmit genetic information. DNA and RNA are polymers made of nucleotide monomers. Each nucleotide contains a phosphate group, a five-carbon sugar, and a nitrogenous base.

DNA contains deoxyribose and the bases adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine. RNA contains ribose and the bases of adenine, uracil, cytosine, and guanine. A brief introduction to this topic may be found in "[What are Nucleic Acids? Nucleic Acid Structure & Function](https://youtu.be/lm14Les80Tk?si=-CBX6D4UbcOEWI3h)".

A diagram showing the structure of nucleotides, each composed of three parts: a phosphate group, a sugar, and a nitrogenous base.

**Figure 4.12:** Nucleotides (OpenStax/Wikimedia Commons/CC BY-SA 3.0)

**B. DNA Structure**

DNA has a sugar-phosphate backbone and paired nitrogenous bases. The two strands are antiparallel, meaning they run in opposite directions.

Base-pairing rules:

- A pair with T

- C pairs with G

**Suggested Time: 25--30 minutes** **FUNCTIONAL GROUPS: pgs. 62-63**

## **Appendix: Molecular Structure of Biological Molecules**

  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Term**                 **Definition**
  ------------------------ --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Amino Acid               A molecule containing an amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen, and variable R group; building blocks of proteins.

  Amino Group              A functional group (-NH2) consisting of nitrogen bonded to hydrogen; found in amino acids.

  Amphipathic              Having both hydrophilic (water-attracting) and hydrophobic (water-repelling) regions.

  Carbohydrate             A biological molecule composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, used for energy and structure.

  Carboxyl Group           A functional group (-COOH) that acts as an acid and is found in many organic molecules.

  Disaccharide             A carbohydrate formed by two monosaccharides linked together by a glycosidic bond.

  Fatty Acid               A lipid component consisting of a carboxyl group and a long hydrocarbon chain.

  Functional Group         A specific group of atoms that gives a molecule its chemical properties.

  Glycosidic Linkage       A covalent bond that joins two monosaccharides in a carbohydrate.

  Hydrolysis               A chemical reaction that breaks bonds by adding water.

  Hydroxyl Group           A functional group (-OH) that is polar and increases solubility in water.

  Lipid                    A group of hydrophobic biological molecules including fats, phospholipids, and sterols.

  Macromolecule            A large biological molecule composed of many smaller subunits.

  Monomer                  A small molecular subunit that can join with others to form a polymer.

  Monosaccharide           A single sugar molecule, such as glucose; the simplest form of carbohydrate.

  Nucleic Acid             A macromolecule (DNA or RNA) that stores and transmits genetic information.

  Nucleotide               The monomer of nucleic acids, consisting of a phosphate group, sugar, and nitrogenous base.

  Peptide Bond             A covalent bond that links amino acids together in proteins.

  Phosphate Group          A functional group (PO4) involved in energy transfer and found in nucleotides.

  Phospholipid             A lipid with a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails that forms cell membranes.

  Polymer                  A large molecule made of repeating monomer units.

  Polysaccharide           A carbohydrate composed of many linked monosaccharides.

  Protein                  A macromolecule made of amino acid chains that performs various cellular functions.

  R Group                  The variable side chain of an amino acid that determines its properties.

  Saturated Fatty Acid     A fatty acid with no double bonds, resulting in a straight chain.

  Sterol                   A lipid with a four-ring carbon structure, such as cholesterol.

  Triglyceride             A lipid composed of glycerol and three fatty acids, used for energy storage.

  Unsaturated Fatty Acid   A fatty acid containing one or more double bonds causing bends in the chain.
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
